items.prompt: What is a "stated objection"?
choices: The reason a buyer gives out loud for not moving forward, which may or may not be the actual deciding factor
A formal written rejection of a proposal
A legal document listing reasons a contract was cancelled
The price a buyer is willing to pay, stated explicitly
items.explanation: A stated objection is simply what's said out loud — the unit's core point is that it's often not the same as what's actually driving the decision.
items.reference:
🗣️ Stated objection — what's said out loud
🔍 Real objection — what's actually driving the decision

Why: these two can differ, and the whole unit is about recognizing when they do.

items.prompt: Is a stated objection always the same as the buyer's actual deciding factor, per this unit?
choices: No — it may or may not be the real reason; the unit's framework is about recognizing when it isn't
Yes — buyers always state their true reasoning directly
No — stated objections are always lies with no basis in truth
Yes, but only in business-to-business sales, never in other contexts
items.explanation: The unit is careful to note that stated objections aren't always covers — sometimes they are the real reason — the skill is recognizing the pattern when it applies, not assuming it always does.
items.reference:
🗣️ Stated objection — what's said out loud
🔍 Real objection — what's actually driving the decision

Why: these two can differ, and the whole unit is about recognizing when they do.

items.prompt: What is a "real objection"?
choices: The actual underlying concern driving a "no" or a stall, often about risk, authority, or internal politics rather than the product itself
A legally binding reason for rejecting a contract
The objection a buyer states in writing rather than verbally
A synonym for "stated objection" — the two terms mean the same thing
items.explanation: The real objection is what actually drives the decision — frequently personal or political, and frequently different from whatever gets said out loud.
items.reference:
🎭 Often about — risk, authority, internal politics
🚫 Rarely about — the product's features alone

Why: knowing what real objections tend to be about is what makes them recognizable and addressable.

items.prompt: According to this unit, what do real objections tend to be about, more often than the product itself?
choices: Risk, authority, and internal politics
The exact color scheme of the product's user interface
The vendor's office location
The number of years the vendor has been in business
items.explanation: The unit consistently frames real objections around the buyer's personal exposure — risk to their reputation, whether they actually have approval authority, or internal political dynamics.
items.reference:
🎭 Often about — risk, authority, internal politics
🚫 Rarely about — the product's features alone

Why: knowing what real objections tend to be about is what makes them recognizable and addressable.

items.prompt: What is "risk aversion," as this unit defines it?
choices: A buyer's reluctance to be the one responsible if a new choice turns out badly, even when the new choice is probably better than the status quo
A general dislike of any financial risk in personal investments
A legal requirement for businesses to avoid risky contracts
The tendency to always choose the cheapest available option
items.explanation: Risk aversion here is specifically about personal accountability — the fear of being blamed if a recommendation goes wrong, even when the recommendation is objectively sound.
items.reference:
⚠️ Risk aversion — fear of being blamed if a new choice goes wrong
🎯 Even when — the new choice is probably better

Why: this is exactly what surfaced in the opening scenario's follow-up call — a genuinely better product still triggers this fear.

items.prompt: Why might a buyer hesitate on a product that's objectively better and cheaper than what they currently have?
choices: Because they're weighing their own personal risk in recommending it, not just comparing the product's features and price
Because better and cheaper products are always scams
Because buyers never actually want to save money
Because objectively better products are technically impossible to identify
items.explanation: The buyer isn't just evaluating the product — they're evaluating their own exposure if the decision goes badly, which a purely rational product comparison doesn't capture.
items.reference:
⚠️ Risk aversion — fear of being blamed if a new choice goes wrong
🎯 Even when — the new choice is probably better

Why: this is exactly what surfaced in the opening scenario's follow-up call — a genuinely better product still triggers this fear.

items.prompt: What is "status quo bias"?
choices: The tendency to prefer what's already being done over a new option, even a clearly better one, because the current approach's flaws are already familiar
A legal bias in favor of existing contracts over new ones
The tendency to always choose the newest available technology
A cognitive bias that only affects senior executives
items.explanation: Status quo bias favors the familiar, survivable flaws of the current approach over the unknown flaws of something new — even when the new option is genuinely better.
items.reference:
😌 Current approach — flaws are known and survivable
❓ New approach — flaws are unknown

Why: "we're happy with what we have" often reflects this bias more than genuine satisfaction.

items.prompt: Per L2's table, which stated objection is most closely associated with status quo bias?
choices: "We're happy with what we have."
"It's a bit expensive for us right now."
"It's not the right time."
"We need to think about it."
items.explanation: L2's table maps this specific stated objection to status quo bias — preferring the familiar current setup over an unfamiliar, even superior, alternative.
items.reference:
😌 Current approach — flaws are known and survivable
❓ New approach — flaws are unknown

Why: "we're happy with what we have" often reflects this bias more than genuine satisfaction.

items.prompt: In the opening scenario, what made the client's "we'll think about it" response confusing to the vendor?
choices: The pitch solved the client's exact stated problem and cost less than their current approach
The client had never heard of monitoring tools before
The vendor's pitch was full of factual errors
The client explicitly said the product was worse than competitors
items.explanation: The scenario is built around the puzzle of a seemingly ideal match between problem and solution still not producing a yes — exactly the situation the unit's framework addresses.
items.reference:
😤 Stated problem — "we don't know when things break"
✅ Pitch — solves it exactly, cheaper too
🤷 Response — "we'll think about it"

Why: a perfect product-problem match still stalling is the entire puzzle this unit exists to explain.

items.prompt: What question does the opening scenario end on?
choices: If the stated problem and the solution line up this well, what's actually stopping the yes?
Should the vendor lower the price further?
Did the client actually understand the product's features?
Was the pitch given in the wrong format?
items.explanation: This closing question sets up the entire unit's central puzzle — a good product-problem fit alone doesn't guarantee a yes, because something else is also being weighed.
items.reference:
😤 Stated problem — "we don't know when things break"
✅ Pitch — solves it exactly, cheaper too

items.prompt: L2 explicitly asks whether its stated-objection-to-real-objection table means every objection is a cover story. What's the answer?
choices: No — sometimes "it's expensive" really does just mean the budget isn't there; the table describes common patterns, not a universal rule
Yes — every stated objection in the table is always false
Yes — buyers are never being honest when they state an objection
The table doesn't address this question at all
items.explanation: L2 is explicit that the table is a set of patterns to listen for, not a claim that deception is universal — some stated objections genuinely are the whole story.
items.reference:
StatedCommon real objection
"Need to think about it"Risk aversion
"Not the right time"Lacks approval authority

Why: treating the table as a universal rule would lead to reading hidden motives into every honest "no," which L2 explicitly warns against.

The vendor's contract terms are illegal

items.prompt: According to L2's flowchart, what two inputs feed into a buyer's actual purchase decision?
choices: The product comparison (better + cheaper) AND the buyer's personal risk (reputation, authority, internal politics)
Only the price of the product, nothing else
Only the buyer's personal opinion of the salesperson
Only the length of the sales pitch
items.explanation: L2's flowchart explicitly shows two separate inputs converging on the buyer's decision — the product comparison and the buyer's personal risk — with only the product comparison typically showing up in the stated objection.
items.reference:
📊 Product comparison — better, cheaper
⚠️ Personal risk — reputation, authority, politics
➡️ Both feed the decision — only the first usually gets stated

Why: the stated objection is an incomplete window into the real decision, missing exactly the second input.

items.prompt: Per L2's flowchart, why does the stated objection almost always reference the product, even when personal risk is the bigger factor?
choices: Because referencing the product is the comfortable, professional-sounding thing to say, while personal risk rarely gets said out loud unprompted
Because personal risk never actually influences purchase decisions
Because buyers are legally required to only discuss product features
Because product-related objections are always the honest, complete truth
items.explanation: L2 explains this directly — talking about the product is socially easy, while admitting to personal risk or lack of authority is not, so the stated objection skews toward the product even when it isn't the deciding factor.
items.reference:
📊 Product comparison — better, cheaper
⚠️ Personal risk — reputation, authority, politics
➡️ Both feed the decision — only the first usually gets stated

Why: the stated objection is an incomplete window into the real decision, missing exactly the second input.

items.prompt: What specific question does L2 recommend asking to surface the real objection?
choices: "What would need to be true for this to be an easy yes?"
"Is that the real reason you're saying no?"
"Why are you lying to me about the price?"
"Don't you think this product is obviously better?"
items.explanation: This forward-looking, non-accusatory question is L2's specific recommended framing — it invites the buyer to name what's missing without putting them on the defensive.
items.reference:
❌ "Is that the real reason?" — accusatory, defensive
✅ "What would need to be true...?" — forward-looking, invites honesty

Why: the framing of the question is what makes it possible to get an honest answer without confrontation.

items.prompt: Why does L2 say "is that the real reason?" is a worse question than "what would need to be true for this to be an easy yes?"
choices: It puts the buyer on the defensive and assumes they were being dishonest, making them less likely to open up
It's grammatically incorrect and confusing to buyers
It takes significantly longer to say out loud
It's illegal to ask in most sales contexts
items.explanation: L2 is explicit that accusatory framing invites defensiveness rather than honesty — the whole point of the alternative question is avoiding that dynamic.
items.reference:
❌ "Is that the real reason?" — accusatory, defensive
✅ "What would need to be true...?" — forward-looking, invites honesty

Why: the framing of the question is what makes it possible to get an honest answer without confrontation.

items.prompt: Per L2, why does asking about the future ("what would need to be true") work better than asking "why not"?
choices: "Why not" asks the buyer to justify a decision already made, inviting them to defend the stated objection more firmly, while a future-oriented question is a planning question, not a justification demand
"Why not" is grammatically incorrect in most languages
Future-oriented questions are always shorter to answer
There is no actual difference between the two framings
items.explanation: L2 draws this exact distinction — a backward-looking question asks for justification of a past decision, while a forward-looking question asks about planning, which is easier to answer honestly.
items.reference:
⏪ "Why not?" — justify a past decision, invites defending it
⏩ "What would need to be true?" — a planning question about the future

Why: the direction the question points (past vs. future) changes whether it invites defense or honesty.

items.prompt: What kind of question does L2 classify "what would need to be true for this to be an easy yes?" as?
choices: A planning question, not a justification demand
A legal disclosure requirement
A rhetorical question with no real answer expected
An accusation phrased as a question
items.explanation: L2 specifically frames this question as forward-looking and planning-oriented, distinct from a demand to justify a decision already made.
items.reference:
⏪ "Why not?" — justify a past decision, invites defending it
⏩ "What would need to be true?" — a planning question about the future

Why: the direction the question points (past vs. future) changes whether it invites defense or honesty.

items.prompt: In L3's follow-up call, what did the client's real objection turn out to be?
choices: Personal risk — being the one who'd recommended switching vendors, and being blamed if the migration caused disruption in the first month
The tool's price was too high compared to competitors
The client had already signed with a different vendor
The vendor's sales team was unresponsive to emails
items.explanation: L3's follow-up conversation reveals the client's real concern was personal exposure during rollout, not anything about the product's price or capability — exactly the kind of real objection L2's framework predicts.
items.reference:
❓ Question asked — "what would need to be true for an easy yes?"
💬 Real objection revealed — personal risk if the migration disrupts anything

Why: this is L3's concrete demonstration of L2's framework actually surfacing a real objection in a live conversation.

items.prompt: What question did the vendor ask in L3's follow-up call, and why that one specifically?
choices: "What would need to be true for this to be an easy yes on your end?" — a forward-looking, non-accusatory question, not "did you make a decision" or "is something else going on"
"Why haven't you responded to my emails?"
"Are you working with a competitor instead?"
"Can you approve this today?"
items.explanation: L3 explicitly contrasts the actual question asked with two worse alternatives (a yes/no stall-inviter, and an implicit accusation) to show why this specific framing worked.
items.reference:
❓ Question asked — "what would need to be true for an easy yes?"
💬 Real objection revealed — personal risk if the migration disrupts anything

Why: this is L3's concrete demonstration of L2's framework actually surfacing a real objection in a live conversation.

items.prompt: Once the real objection was known, what did the vendor offer in L3 — and why not a discount or more features?
choices: A parallel pilot running alongside the existing monitoring with zero changes until the client personally verified it worked — because the concern was rollout risk, not price or capability
A 50% discount on the first year of service
A longer product demo with more technical detail
A free upgrade to a more expensive tier of the product
items.explanation: L3 is explicit that a discount or more features wouldn't address rollout risk — the parallel pilot directly removes the specific exposure the client was worried about.
items.reference:
🎯 Real concern — rollout risk, not price or capability
✅ Response — parallel pilot, zero changes until personally verified

Why: the response has to match the actual concern uncovered, not default to a generic sales lever like discounting.

items.prompt: Why does L3 say the parallel pilot directly answers the client's real objection?
choices: It removes the exact risk the client was worried about — nothing changes about the current monitoring until they've personally seen the new tool work, so there's no window where switching could cause the feared disruption
Because pilots are always cheaper than a full purchase
Because pilots are a standard industry requirement for all vendors
Because it makes the vendor look more trustworthy in general, regardless of the client's specific concern
items.explanation: L3 traces a direct line from the specific real objection (fear of disruption during rollout) to the specific fix (a zero-risk parallel period) — a generic trust-building gesture wouldn't have this precise match.
items.reference:
🎯 Real concern — rollout risk, not price or capability
✅ Response — parallel pilot, zero changes until personally verified

Why: the response has to match the actual concern uncovered, not default to a generic sales lever like discounting.

items.prompt: Per L3, could a better original pitch have surfaced the client's real objection without a follow-up call?
choices: Not reliably — the client likely hadn't consciously framed their own hesitation as "reputational risk from rollout timing" until asked a question that required articulating it
Yes — a sufficiently detailed pitch always surfaces every buyer concern upfront
Yes, but only if the pitch included a lower price from the very start
No — buyer psychology never changes regardless of how a pitch is delivered
items.explanation: L3 makes a subtle but important point: the real objection isn't always a hidden truth being deliberately withheld — sometimes the buyer themselves hasn't put it into words until prompted by the right question.
items.reference:
🤔 Not always hidden on purpose — the buyer may not have consciously framed it yet
❓ The right question — surfaces it for both people at once

Why: this reframes "finding the real objection" as collaborative discovery, not detective work against a withholding buyer.

items.prompt: What does L3 suggest about whether buyers are always deliberately withholding their real objection?

Yes — buyers are always deliberately hiding the truth from vendors

items.explanation: L3 explicitly frames this as sometimes being genuine self-discovery for the buyer, not just information being intentionally concealed — a meaningfully different (and less adversarial) way to think about the interaction.

🤔 Not always hidden on purpose — the buyer may not have consciously framed it yet
❓ The right question — surfaces it for both people at once

items.prompt: L3's extend-it question asks what happens if the real objection had instead been "I don't have the authority to approve this — my boss does." Would the parallel-pilot offer still be the right response?
choices: Probably not — an authority problem needs a structurally different fix, like involving the actual decision-maker directly, not reducing rollout risk which was never the actual concern
Yes — a parallel pilot always solves every possible real objection regardless of what it is
Yes, because pilots are a universal fix for all buyer hesitation
No — in that case, nothing at all could ever be done to move the deal forward
items.explanation: This is exactly the point of the extend-it question: the fix has to match the diagnosis, and an authority problem calls for a different intervention (like getting the actual decision-maker into the conversation) than a risk-based pilot.
items.reference:
🎯 Original real objection — rollout risk → parallel pilot fixes it
❓ Different real objection — lacks authority → needs a different kind of fix entirely

Why: this is L3's own extend-it question — testing whether the reader can apply the framework to a genuinely different diagnosis, not just recall the original fix.
